h: Bascules, blue paint and the best seat on the river
p: Tower Bridge was designed by Sir Horace Jones and the engineer John Wolfe Barry and took around eight years to build, opening in 1894. The two huge roadways, called bascules, lift to let tall ships pass underneath, and seeing them rise is a proper London moment. Lift times are published in advance, so if you'd love to watch one, plan your visit around them and grab a spot along the riverbank.

The high walkways weren't always a tourist attraction. They were originally built so pedestrians could keep crossing while the bridge was raised, but most people just waited for the bridge to come down rather than climbing all those stairs, and they were closed in 1910. They reopened in 1982 as part of the visitor experience, and the glass floors came much later. Its familiar blue and white colour scheme was introduced in 1977 to mark the Queen's Silver Jubilee.

Allow around an hour and a half for the walkways and the engine rooms. The original steam engines were replaced by electricity in the 1970s, but the old engines have been kept in beautiful condition and you can see them up close.

On the south side, Potters Fields Park is a great spot for a picnic with a view of the bridge and the Tower. Shad Thames, a cobbled street of old warehouses linked by iron walkways, is lovely for a stroll and a bite to eat. HMS Belfast, a Second World War cruiser now run as a museum, is moored a short walk west, and St Katharine Docks is just over the bridge on the north side.
